trustRoles.boundary: A verified Pulsar device may create, store, unwrap and use content secrets for epochs and grants it is authorized to access.
The coordinator may route signed public membership state, ciphertext, recipient wraps and documented metadata but must not create, unwrap, escrow, log or recover content secrets.

Coordinator-issued identity alone is insufficient for a verified-device claim; device changes and inconsistent views require client-visible verification or an independently reviewed consistency mechanism.
Primary storage, backups and traffic captures retain opaque protected bytes and disclosed metadata only.
Moderators cannot decrypt protected media unless a recipient deliberately attaches a purpose-limited evidence copy.
Telegram has already seen uploaded plaintext; Spotify playback or control remains provider-side and is never covered by the Pulsar E2EE claim.

attackerClasses.guarantee: Protected content confidentiality and integrity; traffic and retained metadata remain visible as disclosed.
Cannot obtain protected plaintext or content secrets from normal routing, storage, backup, history or observability state.
Cannot decrypt or inject content accepted as an honest sender; withholding, delay and denial of service are not prevented. Forks, stale epochs and replays must fail or become detectable.

Credential or device-set equivocation must be detectable and must block the verified E2EE claim. Prevention requires the separately reviewed device-verification or consistency design; MLS alone is not treated as sufficient.
Cannot forge another verified sender or decrypt epochs outside its authorized membership, but can retain, record, copy or disclose every plaintext and key legitimately received while authorized.
Compromise exposes that endpoint's accessible plaintext and key state; future security can return only after removal, fresh client-owned rotation and honest state update.
Recovery without a surviving authorized device or explicit user-held recovery capability may be impossible; history is not silently escrowed.
No confidentiality claim while malware, an administrator, accessibility abuse, a debugger or another process can read active endpoint plaintext, memory, screen, audio or keystrokes.
E2EE cannot prevent an authorized recipient from recording speakers, copying files or otherwise capturing rendered plaintext.
E2EE does not promise delivery, anonymity, membership hiding, constant-size traffic, timing hiding or denial-of-service resistance.

mediaPaths.claim: Allowed only for an item carried by the reviewed protected container and negotiated e2ee_media_v1 path.
Allowed only for authenticated seekable chunks and manifest fields under the protected path.
A cue inherits the protection state of its exact immutable media revision; a label alone never upgrades it.
Allowed only for fresh authenticated session keys and frames authenticated before jitter decode.
Never described as Pulsar end-to-end encrypted.
Never described as protected by Pulsar E2EE.
No silent plaintext downgrade; the user explicitly excludes unsupported targets or the send fails.
The UI must disclose that the selected plaintext copy leaves E2EE and becomes accessible to moderation under purpose, ACL, audit and retention controls.

requirements.text: Keep e2ee_media_v1 absent or disabled until threat model, both spikes, protocol design review, cross-platform vectors and implementation review close critical/high findings.
Create content, session, device and group secrets only on Pulsar clients and keep them out of coordinator rows, logs, traces, metrics, crash reports and backups.
Treat coordinator delivery and storage as malicious for confidentiality and integrity while excluding delivery availability and traffic-analysis resistance.
Bind each device key to an actor-visible device identity and expose verification state, fingerprint or safety code, and device-change warnings.
Do not treat coordinator-issued credentials alone as peer verification; inconsistent device or epoch views must fail closed and produce a privacy-safe diagnostic.
Require client-owned signed membership commits and fresh epoch entropy for join, leave, role removal, credential revoke and suspected compromise.
Authenticate group, epoch, sender device, immutable target snapshot, media identity, container version and chunk or frame position; reject mismatch before plaintext release.
Provide application-level replay, fork, stale-epoch, generation and downgrade handling; do not assume AEAD or HPKE supplies these policies.
Use unique nonces under every key across devices, crashes and restarts, with deterministic domain separation for media chunks, live frames, wraps and exports.
Never silently send protected content to an unsupported Telegram, Spotify, legacy or mixed-version target.
A removed member cannot receive or derive keys for later epochs, but revoke and delete copy must not claim to erase previously obtained keys, plaintext or recordings.
A new device receives no protected history without an explicit scoped history grant from a surviving authorized device or reviewed recovery capability.
Recovery without surviving authorization or user-held recovery capability is allowed to end in irreversible protected-history loss; coordinator escrow is forbidden.
Bound and wipe local plaintext, decrypt cache, temporary files, pasteboard state and obsolete keys on success, cancel, crash recovery, sign-out, revoke and uninstall where the OS permits.
A malicious or compromised authorized member is allowed by the model to exfiltrate received plaintext; product copy must not promise otherwise.
A voluntary report evidence copy requires recipient intent, an exact preview and disclosure, purpose limitation, least-privilege moderation ACL, audit, short retention and delete flow.
Moderation, analytics, search and observability have no hidden decrypt or key export path; capability loss is disclosed rather than bypassed.
Each media item exposes its actual protection state; UI, Telegram, Store and policy copy cannot infer E2EE from room privacy, TLS, authentication or an unrelated passing capability.
Encrypt clips, tracks and saved cues with an authenticated seekable container and protect live PTT with separate fresh session keys and authenticated bounded frames.
Delete obsolete keys promptly enough for claimed forward secrecy and require an honest post-compromise update before claiming future recovery.
Use secure transport despite message-level protection to reduce exposed membership metadata and network manipulation.
No primitive, algorithm suite, library, key-transparency design or container is selected by this threat-model task; downstream spikes and independent review own those decisions.

C4.claim: After B is removed and the accepted client-owned commit advances the epoch, B cannot decrypt later clips, tracks, cues or live PTT; a new D receives no earlier history without an explicit grant.

C5.claim: Coordinator storage, backups, logs and captured traffic cannot produce playable protected content, while the observed metadata exactly matches the disclosure inventory.

C6.claim: A recipient can deliberately export one disclosed evidence copy into the moderation workflow without any coordinator or moderator decrypt capability.

allowedOnlyAfterAllGates: End-to-end encrypted between the verified Pulsar devices shown for this item.
The coordinator routes this protected item but cannot read its audio content.
This report copy leaves end-to-end encryption and will be available to authorized moderators.
requiredLimitations: Telegram uploads and deliveries are not Pulsar end-to-end encrypted.
Removing a member or deleting an item cannot erase copies, keys or recordings already obtained by another device.
Protected history may be irrecoverable without a surviving authorized device or user-held recovery capability.
Size, duration, timing, participants, targets and delivery metadata remain visible as documented.
forbidden: all Pulsar audio is end-to-end encrypted
the coordinator can never add or substitute a device
moderators can inspect protected content without a report copy
TLS or a private Air means end-to-end encrypted
unsupported targets transparently fall back to plaintext

residualRisks.risk: Coordinator and network traffic analysis reveals the documented metadata and can deny service.
A malicious identity authority can attempt device-set equivocation until the reviewed verification or consistency mechanism detects it.
Authorized, compromised or malicious recipients can retain and redistribute plaintext.
Endpoint or OS compromise exposes active plaintext, audio, memory and available keys.
Loss of every authorized device and recovery capability can permanently lose protected history.
A voluntary moderation evidence copy creates a new controlled plaintext copy.
Ciphertext retained in backups remains exposed to future cryptanalytic or implementation failures.
Security depends on correct library integration, randomness, nonce discipline, key deletion and constant-time implementations.

sources.use: MLS trust roles, malicious delivery service, identity service compromise, membership, recovery, metadata, endpoint compromise and replay limits.
Client-owned epochs, current-member entropy, transport metadata, authentication and bounded generation handling.
HPKE is not selected here; its documented lack of replay, downgrade and length hiding constrains any downstream use.
AEAD nonce uniqueness, authenticated associated data and the fact that AEAD does not provide access control or replay policy.
Internet attacker model with network control.
Non-normative data-centric threat-model structure; explicitly not treated as a final standard.
